title: Leaders Learn by Changing What They Notice
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article offers concrete techniques for leaders to see familiar environments with fresh eyes, treating noticing as a trainable skill rather than a fixed trait. It suggests changing physical vantage points, deliberately focusing on peripheral or overlooked details, and drawing on author Rob Walker's idea of noticing 'ghosts and ruins' — traces of past practices that reveal how an organization really works. Another technique described is temporarily adopting an unfamiliar persona, like a historian or investor, while observing a situation, which surfaces questions a leader's habitual role would never prompt. The piece closes by framing regular noticing practice as a way of clearing mental clutter so insight has room to emerge.
points: Noticing is described as a trainable skill leaders can practice through small, concrete prompts.
Changing physical or mental vantage point is the most common way to catch what habitual viewpoints miss.
Focusing on peripheral, non-obvious details, or Rob Walker's 'ghosts and ruins,' often reveals more than the obvious focal point.
Temporarily adopting an unfamiliar persona while observing surfaces new questions and angles.
Regular noticing practice clears mental clutter and creates room for genuine insight.
quotes: An occasional 'mind cleanse' is essential for critical and creative thinking.
Probably the most common advice for seeing things anew is for leaders to change their vantage point.
He suggests leaders should notice 'ghosts and ruins,' his words for the traces of the past that remain in place, like abandoned features or faded uses.
When leaders view matters from different personas, they focus on issues and ask the questions those roles require of them.
The idea is to interrupt entrenched habits long enough to let something true come into view.
